opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as asking what survives of the DreamCoder idea once you have a pretrained language model sitting in the middle.

DreamCoder had two core intuitions. First, you learn by alternating between solving problems, the wake phase, and consolidating what you learned, the sleep phase. Second, the consolidation should change the prior over programs, so things that were hard to find become easy. In DreamCoder that meant growing a symbolic library of reusable abstractions and training a neural recognition model on replays and fantasies, programs sampled from the current library and run to make synthetic tasks.

What changed is that the prior no longer has to be built from scratch. A language model trained on enormous amounts of code already has a rich, if messy, sense of what programs people write. So the question in the work with Wen-Ding was: can we keep the wake-sleep loop but let the LLM be both the proposal distribution and the thing being adapted?

Roughly: in the wake phase, you sample many candidate programs from the model, execute them, and keep the ones consistent with the examples. Execution is a hard filter, which is a huge advantage of program induction over pure transduction. You aren't trusting the network's guess; you're checking it. Then the sleep phase looks a lot like DreamCoder's fantasies. You sample programs, run them to get input-output pairs, and fine-tune on those. Because the programs come from the model and are verified by an interpreter, the training data is correct by construction, even if the distribution is a bit odd.

The interesting part is that the self-generated data is grounded in a particular domain. A generic code model knows Python, but it doesn't know the idioms of, say, ARC-style grid puzzles or a quirky list-processing DSL. Fine-tuning on its own verified successes and fantasies pulls the prior toward that domain, and you see real gains in sample efficiency, which is the same thing we saw in DreamCoder, where later tasks became cheap once the right concepts were learned.

There are things I'm less satisfied with. DreamCoder's library learning was explicit. You could open the library and see a concept like "map" or "fold" that the system had invented. When the adaptation lives in fine-tuned weights, the abstractions are implicit and harder to inspect or compose. Part of me thinks the right synthesis has both: the LLM as a flexible prior, plus an explicit, growing library it can call, so knowledge is reusable and interpretable rather than smeared across parameters.

The other lesson, which came through in our work on ARC, is that induction isn't the whole story. Some problems are naturally solved by writing a program, and others are better solved by directly predicting the output, more perceptual and less algorithmic. Those two modes turned out to be surprisingly complementary; they solve different problems. So I don't see it as program synthesis versus neural nets. It's about building systems that know when to reason explicitly in code and when to trust intuition, and that keep improving through something like a wake-sleep cycle.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that DreamCoder had this really nice loop, this wake-sleep cycle, where you alternate between solving problems and then consolidating what you learned from solving them into a library of reusable concepts and a neural recognition model. The problem was that the whole thing was built on this very hand-engineered, lambda-calculus-style DSL, and the search was essentially enumerative. So it scaled to the kinds of domains we put in the paper, but it was never going to scale to, say, writing real Python.

What Wen-Ding and I wanted to do was keep the spirit of that loop and swap out the machinery. The core idea in the work with him is that you take a pretrained language model, which already knows an enormous amount about programs, and you treat it as the proposal distribution. Given input-output examples, it samples candidate programs. That's the "wake" phase, in DreamCoder terms. And then the "sleep" part is where it gets interesting. We can run those programs, check them against the examples, and we have a verifier for free. So every problem we solve becomes a training signal, and we fine-tune the model on its own successful solutions. That's the self-improvement loop, and it's really the same thing as DreamCoder's dreaming, just with gradient descent on a transformer instead of fitting a small recognition network.

The other piece that carries over, and I think this is underappreciated, is the fantasy data. In DreamCoder we would sample programs from the current library, execute them, and train the recognition model on those imagined tasks. You can do exactly the same thing with an LLM. You ask it to generate programs and inputs, you run them to get outputs, and now you have an unbounded supply of synthetic program induction problems that are, by construction, solvable. And because the model's prior shifts as it learns, the distribution of fantasies shifts too, so it bootstraps.

What we lose, honestly, is the explicit library. DreamCoder would give you back a concept like "fold" or "map" that a human could read. With a fine-tuned LLM, that knowledge is implicit in the weights. I go back and forth on whether that matters. For raw performance it probably doesn't, and the LLM version is dramatically more general. For interpretability and for the cognitive science story about how people build up abstractions, I think we still want something library-like, and that's a direction I'm pretty actively thinking about. But as a way of getting wake-sleep into the era of large models, I think the induction work is the natural successor. It's the same algorithm at the level of ideas, with the parts that didn't scale replaced by parts that do.

astra-6.text:
I think the connection is that we want a program synthesizer to get better through experience. In DreamCoder, you alternate between solving problems and learning from those solutions. You learn reusable pieces of code, and you train a neural network to guide the search. Those two things reinforce each other: the library makes useful programs easier to express, and the neural network makes them easier to find.

With program induction by example, the task is to infer a program from examples of its behavior. A natural way to bring in the sleep phase is to run that process backward: generate a program, execute it to produce input-output examples, and then train a model to recover the program from those examples. You can manufacture training problems where you know a correct solution, without requiring someone to annotate every task.

But the important part of the DreamCoder connection is closing the loop. If you just generate a fixed dataset of random programs, you’re learning to solve whatever distribution your generator happens to produce. You’d like the problems you actually encounter—and the solutions you discover—to influence what you generate and learn from next.

So I see modern language models as a powerful starting point for that process. They already provide a lot of knowledge about code. The question is how to turn that starting point into a system that continually improves its proposals, checks them through execution, and builds on what it has successfully learned.

sol-6.1.text:
The connection I’d draw is that program induction from examples has two problems that really need to be solved together. One is finding a program that explains the examples. The other is learning what kinds of programs are worth looking for in the first place.

In DreamCoder, that becomes a wake-sleep loop. During waking, you try to solve tasks with your current library and your current search procedure. Then you use those solutions to improve the system: you discover reusable abstractions, and you train a recognition model to guide future search. You can also generate programs and their input-output examples to give that recognition model more training data.

So the way I think about the work with Wen-Ding is as bringing that feedback loop into a setting where you have much stronger learned models for proposing programs. But proposing a plausible program isn’t sufficient. You still want to execute it, check it against the examples, and use search to resolve the places where the model is uncertain.

The interesting question is whether solving tasks makes the system a better synthesizer afterward. Can it take something that initially required a lot of search and turn it into a reusable piece of knowledge—an abstraction, or an improvement in its proposal distribution—so that the next related problem becomes easier? That’s the central idea I’d want to preserve from DreamCoder.
